title.zh: 高瓦之隱箭：疾病與死亡

region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（欽韋區）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi (!Kung) oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1960s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall, published 1976

source.archive: Harvard University Press (book); ethnographic film archive
source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi

texts.license: Paraphrase for educational use; underlying recordings remain with the Marshall family and Ju/'hoan community

summary.en: Among the Ju/'hoansi illness and death come from !Gauwa, the great god who shoots people with invisible arrows from ambush or sends ghosts to do it. The arrows lodge unseen in the body; sickness grows as they fester; and only the trancing healers, who die and rise within the dance, can see and draw them out. !Gauwa owns the eland and all the big game, and men plead with him for animals as they plead for health.
summary.zh: 朱霍安西人中，疾病與死亡皆出於大神高瓦：他自埋伏處以隱形之箭射人，或遣鬼為之。箭匿體內，病隨之發；唯入迷之醫者——於舞中死而復生者——能見之拔之。高瓦掌大羚與群獸；獵者為獸如為健康而懇求於他。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan religious knowledge recorded by ethnographers with community cooperation; presented as documented paraphrase, not as community speech.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976), chs. on religion and illness; not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi hold that !Gauwa (|Gauwa), the great god, shoots people with invisible arrows — from his own hand, or through the ghosts of the dead which he sends. The arrows enter the body unseen and lie there; the sickness grows as they work, and a person dies when !Gauwa has shot him finally, or when a ghost has come to take him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. Ghosts (the spirits of dead Ju) are blamed for many deaths; they belong to !Gauwa and do his shooting. A sick person may say that a ghost came to him at night, or that !Gauwa has shot him; the family debates which of the two it was, for the treatment — and the blame — differ. Only the healers (n/um k’iaosi, 'owners of n/um') can see the arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); not verbatim. In the great medicine dances the healers trance, die for a moment, and rise to lay hands on the sick: they see !Gauwa's arrows glittering in the patient's body, seize them, and pull them out, flinging them back toward the darkness. !Gauwa also owns the eland and the big game; hunters who fail say he has hidden his animals, and plead with him as they plead for health.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); not verbatim.

title.en: The !Gauwasi: Ancestors Who Shoot from the Dark
title.zh: 高瓦西：暗處射人之祖靈

region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝地區（波札那與納米比亞交界）（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San: Men, Women, and Work in a Foraging Society (1979); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The Ju dead become !Gauwasi, spirits of the dead who live in holes in rocks and trees and are subject to !Gauwa. They shoot the living with invisible arrows, they frighten lonely travellers, and they are treated with name-avoidance and gifts: their names are never spoken again, food is left at the grave, and the dead person's belongings are broken so no ghost may come for them.
summary.zh: 朱人死者成為高瓦西——居於岩石樹洞之祖靈，受高瓦轄制。彼等以隱箭射生者，嚇孤旅；人們避其名、獻食於墓、毀其遺物，以免其魂來尋。

sensitivity.note: Modern Ju/'hoan belief recorded by ethnographers; presented as documented paraphrase.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9 (Religion and Healing); not verbatim. The !Kung hold that the dead turn into ghosts (!Gauwasi) who dwell in the holes of rocks and baobab trees and are ruled by the great god !Gauwa. The ghosts are feared rather than loved: they are believed to shoot the living with invisible arrows, and to come for the dying.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The name of a dead person is never spoken again by his kin; if the name is that of a common object or animal, the word itself is changed or replaced — so closely is the living tied to the dead. The dead person's hut, bow, mats and cooking gear are broken and burned so that no part of him remains for a ghost to come back for; food is sometimes left at the grave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979) and Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. A widow or widower is smudged and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the ghost of the spouse, who is thought to hover close; the mourners wail a formula that sends the dead away to !Gauwa's country, for the dead who linger too long begin to shoot the living.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: Boiling Energy: The Ju/'hoan Trance Dance
title.zh: 沸騰之力：朱霍安西迷舞

region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi religious practice; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall, Richard Katz and Megan Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy: Community Healing among the Kalahari !Kung (1982); Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976)

summary.en: Around the night fire, women in file sing and stamp the giraffe songs while the men — the owners of n/um, a boiling energy at the base of the spine — dance in a half-circle. The n/um heats, climbs the spine, and the dancers trance: they die for an instant, cross into !Gauwa's country, and rise to draw !Gauwa's arrows out of the sick with their hands, feet, and the smell of burning herbs.
summary.zh: 夜火之畔，女列隊而歌而踏長頸鹿之歌；男者——脊柱基部沸騰之n/um之主——半環而舞。n/um發熱，沿脊上行，舞者入迷：剎那而死，越入高瓦之境，復起以手、足與焚草之氣拔出病者體內高瓦之箭。

sensitivity.note: Ju/'hoan healing practice documented with community participation; paraphrase only, not ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz, Boiling Energy (1982), chs. 1-3; not verbatim. The trance dance (n/um tchai or the giraffe dance) is the central religious institution of the Ju/'hoansi. Women sit in file around the fire singing and clapping the medicine songs — the giraffe song is the great one — while the men dance around them; the singing and the drumming of feet feed the n/um, the medicine power, in the dancers.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. As n/um boils up from the base of the spine, some dancers enter kia, the trance state: they say they die for a moment, that their thoughts travel to !Gauwa's place, and that they come back with the sight to see !Gauwa's arrows in the sick. They lay trembling hands on chests and backs, suck and blow, and pull the arrows out, sometimes staggering and falling; the others steady them and keep them from the fire.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The dance goes on through the night until the sick sleep and the arrows are out; in the morning the camp says who was healed and who was shot too deeply. The dance is also the meeting-place of the whole waterhole group — the social and religious centre of Ju/'hoan life.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

region.zh: 南非德拉肯斯堡山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Southern San rock art (last painted before c. 1900); interpreted 1981-2000 from 19th-century |Xam records

source.archive: Published scholarship drawing on Bleek & Lloyd archive
source.work: David Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing: Symbolic Meanings in Southern San Rock Paintings (1981); Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989)

summary.en: The eland is the great reservoir of n/um potency: in |Xam thought its blood and fat are medicine, and shamans enter trance 'dying' like wounded eland. Lewis-Williams reads the painted eland and the crossed, half-human dancers beside them as the record of the trance dance — potency rising, shamans bleeding from the nose, and the dance-floor of the rock wall.
summary.zh: 大羚為n/um之力之巨庫：|Xam觀念中其血其脂皆藥，薩滿入迷時如傷羚『垂死』。路易斯-威廉斯解讀岩壁之大羚與交叉半人舞者，為迷舞之記——力上升、薩滿鼻血、岩面即舞場。

sensitivity.note: Interpretive archaeology built on the |Xam archive; the eland remains ritually central to San-descended communities.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams, Believing and Seeing (1981), chs. on eland and potency; not verbatim. In |Xam accounts the eland is the embodiment of !gi (potency): its fat and blood are the strongest medicines, and the shaman in trance is said to 'die' and behave like a wounded eland, standing with lowered head, shaking, and bleeding from the nose.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson, Images of Power (1989); not verbatim. Paintings of eland surrounded by elongated, bent-forward human figures with crossed arms and white potency spots are read as shamans dancing around the reservoir of power in trance, their ritual killing of the eland paralleling the trance death. The rock face itself is the veil of the spirit world; the dance is danced against it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams & Dowson (1989); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the same scholarship drawing on Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim. The eland's blood, spilled in the first-kill rites, is believed to make the hunter who eats of it strong and calm; the eland dance at a girl's first menstruation marks her as the eland's bride, and the potency of the animal passes into the band.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lewis-Williams (1981) and Vinnicombe (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Outside the Body: Ju/'hoan Astral Shamans
title.zh: 體外之獅：朱霍安西離體薩滿

region.zh: 喀拉哈里尼亞尼亞／多貝（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1990s by Lorna Marshall, Katz and Guenther

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); Katz (1982)

summary.en: Powerful healers are said to leave their bodies in trance (k’ebu) and travel to far camps, to the dead, or into lions: dying !Gauwa-men become lions, and a lion met on the path may be a shaman out walking. The lion's roar at night may be a sorcerer's spirit calling; the healer who brings his k’ebu back tells where he has been.
summary.zh: 力大之醫者入迷時（克布）離體遠行——至遠村、至死者處、或入獅身：垂死之高瓦之人化為獅，途遇之獅或為外遊之薩滿。夜吼之獅或為巫靈之喚；攜克布歸之醫者能述其所至。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), religion chapters; not verbatim. The !Kung say that a man with strong n/um can, in trance, send his k’ebu — his spirit or shadow-self — out of his body to travel far away, to see what is happening at other waterholes, or to visit !Gauwa and the dead; his body lies as if asleep while his k’ebu is abroad.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999); not verbatim. Lions are intimately linked with trancers: a dying shaman becomes a lion, and a lion met in the bush may be a trance-traveller in lion form; the roar heard at night is sometimes taken for the voice of a !Gauwa-man calling. When a healer returns from trance he tells of his journey — where he went, what he saw, whom he fought.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. In the dance a healer may announce that he has been among the ghosts, or that he has pulled a lion out of a sick person — that the illness was a !Gauwa-man in lion form lodged inside; the extraction and the story together close the case of the illness.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

title.en: The Name That Must Not Be Spoken

region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝／坎瓜（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi custom; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee, published 1979

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After death a Ju/'hoan's name is tabooed forever; kin may not speak it, and if it is an everyday word — 'honey', 'zebra', 'fire' — the word is replaced in the language of that band. The name-taboo follows the ghost into the naming of children and even of jokes, so that the dead are honoured by silence.
summary.zh: 朱人逝者之名永為禁忌；親屬不得言，若其名為常用詞——『蜜』『斑馬』『火』——該詞於其群之語中即遭替換。名諱隨鬼魂延及兒名與戲言；死者以緘默受尊。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. The names of the dead are avoided absolutely: a kinsman will not speak his dead father's or mother's name, and people related by the name-link (children named after the dead) avoid it too. Where the dead person's name was an ordinary word, the band replaces the word — a new word is coined for 'honey' or 'zebra' — so that the name never has to be said again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. The name-taboo is part of the fear and honour owed to the !Gauwasi: speaking the dead person's name invites the ghost, as does handling his belongings. Children named for the dead are said to carry the dead person's 'shade' and must be watched.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Eland Bull Dance at First Menstruation

region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi rite; recorded 1950s-1980s by Lorna Marshall and John Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); John Marshall, films of the Ju/'hoansi (N!ai, 1978)

summary.en: At a girl's first menstruation the camp performs the eland dance: women and men file around her, stroke her arms and shoulders 'the way an eland's mane is stroked', singing the eland songs, so that the potency of the eland bull — !Gauwa's favourite animal — enters her body and makes her strong, fat, and fruitful.
summary.zh: 少女初潮時，營地行大羚之舞：眾人列隊繞之，如撫羚鬣般撫其臂肩，歌大羚之歌——使高瓦至愛之動物大羚牛之力入其身，使其強壯、豐腴、多產。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan puberty rite; paraphrase only, no ritual instruction.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976), ch. on the eland ceremony; not verbatim. When a girl menstruates for the first time the band holds the eland ceremony: the people form a line and dance around her, singing the eland songs; they touch and stroke her arms, shoulders and back — as one strokes the mane of an eland bull — so that the eland's potency enters her.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The eland is !Gauwa's great animal, the reservoir of n/um; the dance is held so that the girl will be strong, that her blood will flow well, and that she will grow fat and bear children well. The rite ends with feasting on eland meat if the hunters have been lucky, and the girl is said now to be 'like an eland'.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Giraffe Song: The Great Medicine of the Dance

region.zh: 喀拉哈里多貝（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi medicine songs; recorded 1950s-1980s by Marshall, Katz and Biesele

source.work: Richard Katz, Boiling Energy (1982); Megan Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: The giraffe song is the strongest of the Ju/'hoan medicine songs: sung at the night dance, its long rising phrases pull the n/um up the dancers' spines and open the deepest trances. The giraffe, like the eland, is an animal of !Gauwa; to sing the giraffe is to call the biggest medicine into the circle.
summary.zh: 長頸鹿之歌為朱霍安西醫歌之至強者：夜舞中其悠揚上揚之句牽動舞者脊中之n/um，開最深之迷。長頸鹿與大羚同為高瓦之獸；唱長頸鹿即召至大之藥入環。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan medicine song; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim. The giraffe dance is the most powerful of the Ju/'hoan medicine dances; the women's song of the giraffe, with its long, rising, circling phrases, is said to pull the n/um hardest up the men's spines, and the deepest trances are entered under this song.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Katz (1982); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele, Women Like Meat (1993); not verbatim. Medicine songs belong to the animals of !Gauwa — eland, giraffe, gemsbok — and each song is 'owned' by the line of healers who inherited it; the songs are the animals' gifts, and singing them correctly is itself a form of hunting the animal's power into the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Biesele (1993); not verbatim.

title.en: Dreams as Visits from the Dead

region.zh: 納米比亞尼亞尼亞（象徵定位）

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi oral tradition; recorded 1950s-1970s by Lorna Marshall

source.work: Lorna Marshall, The !Kung of Nyae Nyae (1976); Lorna Marshall, Nyae Nyae !Kung Beliefs and Rites (1999)

summary.en: Dreams are taken literally: to dream of a dead kinsman is to be visited by his !Gauwasi, who may come in kindness or to shoot. The dreamer wakes the camp, tells the visit, and the healers check the sick list; dreams of !Gauwa himself foretell the deaths he is planning.
summary.zh: 夢境被視為實事：夢見亡親即其高瓦西來訪——或善或射。夢者醒而告營眾，醫者檢視病者名單；夢見高瓦本人者，預示其所謀之死。

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976/1999); not verbatim. The Ju/'hoansi treat dreams as real events: the dead come in dreams because it is the way the !Gauwasi visit; a dream of a dead kinsman may mean he came in kindness, to look at his people, or that he has come to shoot someone in the camp.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same works; not verbatim. A dream of !Gauwa is the gravest: he is said to sit counting his arrows in the dreamer's dream, and each arrow counted is a death he has decided on. In the morning the camp debates the dream, and the healers keep watch over the person the arrows seemed to point at.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: Naro Trickster Tales: The Dassie's Council
title.zh: 納羅詭計故事：蹄兔之議

region.zh: 波札那甘茲區（象徵定位）

texts.period: Naro (Central Kalahari) oral tradition; recorded 1980s-1990s, published in Guenther 1999

source.work: Mathias Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers: Bushman Religion and Society (1999); Guenther, The Naron Bushmen (1986 field corpus)

summary.en: In Naro storytelling the trickster world of Kaggen's descendants lives on: animal tales in which the weak outwit the strong — the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's feints, the lion fooled at his own kill — carry the same message as the old myths: that the small, the hungry and the cunning survive in a world ruled by !Gauwa's arrows and the big game's whims.
summary.zh: 納羅敘事中，卡根後裔之詭計世界猶存：弱者智勝強者之獸故事——岩上蹄兔之議、豺之佯攻、獅受騙於己獲——承古神話之訊：在高瓦之箭與巨獸任性統治之世，唯小者、飢者、狡者得存。

sensitivity.note: Modern Naro oral tradition recorded with community collaboration; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther, Tricksters and Trancers (1999), chs. on Naro folklore; not verbatim. Naro animal tales continue the Kaggen cycle's logic: the trickster is small and vulnerable, and his tricks are responses to hunger and threat; the dassie's council on the rock, the jackal's endless feints, and the lion outwitted at his own kill all teach that the weak survive by cunning.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase, same work; not verbatim. The trickster tales are told at night around the fire and are explicitly entertainment as well as instruction — a Naro speaker says the old stories and the new ones are the same talk, only the animals change; and behind them all stands the same dangerous world of !Gauwa and his arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Guenther (1999); not verbatim.

title.en: Scaring the Ghost: Fire, Ash and the Widower

texts.period: Ju/'hoansi rite; documented 1963-1973 by Richard B. Lee

source.work: Richard B. Lee, The !Kung San (1979), ch. 9; Lorna Marshall (1976)

summary.en: After a death the widow or widower is smudged with ash and medicine smoke, the belongings of the dead are broken, and the camp lights fires at the path so the ghost will not follow the living home. The mourners call the formula that sends the !Gauwasi to !Gauwa's country, and the first nights are kept loud and bright.
summary.zh: 喪禮之後，以灰與藥煙熏寡婦鰥夫，碎毀亡者之物，於歸途燃火，使鬼不隨生者歸家。哀者誦送魂之辭，遣高瓦西赴高瓦之境；初夜喧亮不輟。

sensitivity.note: Documented Ju/'hoan mourning rite; paraphrase only.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979), ch. 9; not verbatim. After the burial the dead person's hut and belongings are broken up and burned; the widowed spouse is smoked and rubbed with ash and medicines to drive off the spouse's ghost, which is thought to hover around and to be able to shoot the survivor with !Gauwa's arrows.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lee (1979); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim. Fires are kept burning on the paths at night so the ghost will not follow the living home; the mourners wail the words that send the dead away to !Gauwa's country, and the camp keeps loud and bright for the first nights, for a quiet dark camp is where a ghost can walk.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Marshall (1976); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hare Reverses the Message (Katkop/Hottentot Version)
title.zh: 野兔逆轉訊息（卡茲科普／霍屯督版）

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: San oral tradition (Katkop dialect); recorded 1875 by !khusin (Bleek & Lloyd); English redaction in Honey 1910

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (1875), §18; James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death'

summary.en: In the messenger form of the myth the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life; but the Hare reverses it into a message of death. The angered Moon heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip — the told-three-times Katkop version recorded by Bleek, and the English redaction printed by Honey.
summary.zh: 訊使版神話中，月遣野兔赴人類報『復生』之訊；野兔反轉為『死亡』之訊。月怒，燒石烙其口，兔唇由此而來——此為布萊克三度採錄之卡茲科普版，亦為霍尼1910年英譯所本。

sensitivity.note: The narrator !khusin's father was Hottentot; Bleek doubts whether this form is original Bushman. Flagged as a border-version of the origin-of-death cluster.

passages.text: The Moon, it is said, sent once an Insect to Men, saying, 'Go thou to Men, and tell them, As I die, and dying live, so ye shall also die, and dying live.' The Insect started with the message, but whilst on his way was overtaken by the Hare, who asked: 'On what errand art thou bound?'... With these words he ran off, and when he reached Men, he said, 'I am sent by the Moon to tell you, As I die, and dying perish, in the same manner ye shall also die and come wholly to an end.'
passages.note: Quote from James A. Honey, South-African Folk-Tales (1910), 'The Origin of Death' (public domain; the tale derives from Bleek 1875 §18).

passages.text: Then the Hare returned to the Moon, and told her what he had said to Men. The Moon reproached him angrily, saying, 'Darest thou tell the people a thing which I have not said?' With these words she took up a piece of wood, and struck him on the nose. Since that day the Hare's nose is slit.
passages.note: Quote from Honey (1910), public domain.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§18): the veritable Hottentot myth of the 'Origin of Death' is told in the Katkop dialect by !khusin, whose father was a Hottentot; although the narrator says he heard the story from his mother \xa-\kho, a Bushwoman, its Hottentot origin can hardly be doubted. Here the Moon sends the Hare to men with the message of the renewal of life, but it reverses it into a message of death; the angered Moon then heats a stone and burns the Hare's mouth, causing the harelip. !khusin told this story three times.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §18; not verbatim.
